This document covers the theory and tools needed for effective fuzzing.\n\n## Key Concepts\n\n### What is Fuzzing?\nFuzzing is a software testing technique that feeds randomly generated or mutation-based inputs to a program to find bugs, crashes, and unexpected behavior. Coverage-guided fuzzing uses code coverage metrics to generate more effective test inputs.\n\n### Coverage-Guided Fuzzing\nIn Python, we simulate LibFuzzer-style fuzzing by:\n1. Creating a fuzz driver function that takes input data\n2. Processing input data through the target library\n3. Measuring code coverage to guide input generation\n4. Using tools like `atheris` or `coverage` to track coverage\n\n## Python Fuzzing Tools\n\n### Atheris\n**What it is:** Official Python fuzzer from Google, integrates libFuzzer for function_to_fuzz\n\n@atheris.instrument_func\ndef test_one(data):\n    # Feed data to target function\n    try:\n        result = function_to_fuzz(data)\n    except Exception:\n        return\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    atheris.Setup(sys.argv, test_one)\n    atheris.Fuzz()\n```\n\n### Libfuzzer (via atheris)\n- LibFuzzer is a coverage-guided, evolutionary fuzzing engine\n- Atheris parse carefully\n    # For numeric inputs\n    if len(data) >= 4:\n        value = int.from_bytes(data[:4], 'little')\n```\n\n### Target Function Selection\nChoose functions that:\n- Accept string, Public API definitions\n- `core.py` or `main.py` - Core functionality\n- `parse.py` or `parser.py` - Parsing logic\n- `utils.py` - Utility functions (often handle edge cases)\n\n**Command to find functions:**\n```bash\ngrep -r \"^def \" --include=\"*.py\" src/\ngrep -r \"^class \" --include=\"*.py\" src/\n```\n\n### Step 5: Entry Point Discovery\n\n```python\n# In Python REPL or script\nimport library_name\n\n# Find public API\npublic_items = [item for item in dir(library_name) if not item.startswith('_')]\nprint(public_items)\n\n# Check for main functions\nfor item in public_items:\n    obj = getattr(library_name, item)\n    if callable(obj):\n        print(f\"{item}: {type(obj)}, docstring: {obj.__doc__[:100]}\")\n```\n\n### Step 6: Input Format Analysis\n\n**Determine expected input:**\n- String? Binary? Structured data?\n- Fixed format or variable length?\n- Character encoding requirements?\n- Special delimiters or markers?\n\n**Example analysis:**\n```bash\n# Check type hints\ngrep -r \"def.*->.*str\" src/\ngrep -r \"def.*->.*bytes\" src/\ngrep -r \"def.*->.*dict\" src/\n\n# Look for parsing patterns\ngrep -r \"split\\|parse\\|loads\\|decode\" src/\ngrep -r \"struct.unpack\\|pickle\\|json\" src/\n```\n\n### Step 7: Error Handling Patterns\n\n**Find expected exceptions:**\n```bash\ngrep -r \"except\\|raise\" --include=\"*.py\" src/ | head -50\n```\n\n**Common exception types:**\n- ValueError - Invalid values\n- TypeError - Wrong type\n- KeyError - Missing keys\n- IndexError - Index out of bounds\n- AttributeError - Missing attributes\n- UnicodeDecodeError - Encoding issues\n\n### Step 8: Version and Dependencies\n\n```bash\ncat setup.py | grep version\ncat setup.py | grep python_requires\npip show library_name\n```\n\n## Example Analysis Template\n\nCreate `notes_for_testing.txt` with:\n\n```\nLibrary: [name]\nPurpose: [one-line description]\nVersion: [version]\nPython: [version requirement]\n\nMAIN ENTRY POINTS:\n1. module.function_name(input_type) -> output_type\n   - Purpose: [what it does]\n   - Input format: [expected format]\n   - Location: [file:line]\n\n2. module.another_function(...)\n   - ...\n\nINPUT FORMATS:\n- Type: [str/bytes/dict/custom]\n- Encoding: [utf-8/binary/other]\n- Structure: [format details]\n- Limits: [min/max length, special requirements]\n\nFUZZ TARGETS (priority order):\n1. [function] - [reason]\n   File: [path]\n   Line: [number]\n\n2. It implements and updates the datetime type, plugging gaps in functionality and providing an intelligent module API that supports many common creation scenarios. Simply put, it helps you work with dates and times with fewer imports and a lot less code.\n    32→\n    33→Arrow is named after the `arrow of time <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrow_of_time>`_ and is heavily inspired by `moment.js <https://github.com/moment/moment>`_ and `requests <https://github.com/psf/requests>`_.\n    34→\n    35→Why use Arrow over built-in modules?\n    36→------------------------------------\n    37→\n    38→Python's standard library and some other low-level modules have near-complete date, time and timezone functionality, but don't work very well from a usability perspective:\n    39→\n    40→- Too many modules: datetime, time, calendar, dateutil, pytz and more\n    41→- Too many types: date, time, datetime, tzinfo, timedelta, relativedelta, etc.\n    42→- Timezones and timestamp conversions are verbose and unpleasant\n    43→- Timezone naivety is the norm\n    44→- Gaps in functionality: ISO 8601 parsing, timespans, humanization\n    45→\n    46→Features\n    47→--------\n    48→\n    49→- Fully-implemented, drop-in replacement for datetime\n    50→- Support for Python 3.8+\n    51→- Timezone-aware and UTC by default\n    52→- Super-simple creation options for many common input scenarios\n    53→- ``shift`` method with support for relative offsets, including weeks\n    54→- Format and parse strings automatically\n    55→- Wide support for the `ISO 8601 <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601>`_ standard\n    56→- Timezone conversion\n    57→- Support for ``dateutil``, ``pytz``, and ``ZoneInfo`` tzinfo objects\n    58→- Generates time spans, ranges, floors and ceilings for time frames ranging from microsecond to year\n    59→- Humanize dates and times with a growing list of contributed locales\n    60→- Extensible for your own Arrow-derived types\n    61→- Full support for PEP 484-style type hints\n    62→\n    63→Quick Start\n    64→-----------\n    65→\n    66→Installation\n    67→~~~~~~~~~~~~\n    68→\n    69→To install Arrow, use `pip <https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/quickstart/>`_ or `pipenv <https://docs.pipenv.org>`_:\n    70→\n    71→.. code-block:: console\n    72→\n    73→    $ pip install -U arrow\n    74→\n    75→Example Usage\n    76→~~~~~~~~~~~~~\n    77→\n    78→.. code-block:: python\n    79→\n    80→    >>> import arrow\n    81→    >>> arrow.get('2013-05-11T21:23:58.970460+07:00')\n    82→    <Arrow [2013-05-11T21:23:58.970460+07:00]>\n    83→\n    84→    >>> utc = arrow.utcnow()\n    85→    >>> utc\n    86→    <Arrow [2013-05-11T21:23:58.970460+00:00]>\n    87→\n    88→    >>> utc = utc.shift(hours=-1)\n    89→    >>> utc\n    90→    <Arrow [2013-05-11T20:23:58.970460+00:00]>\n    91→\n    92→    >>> local = utc.to('US/Pacific')\n    93→    >>> local\n    94→    <Arrow [2013-05-11T13:23:58.970460-07:00]>\n    95→\n    96→    >>> local.timestamp()\n    97→    1368303838.970460\n    98→\n    99→    >>> local.format()\n   100→    '2013-05-11 13:23:58 -07:00'\n   101→\n   102→    >>> local.format('YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss ZZ')\n   103→    '2013-05-11 13:23:58 -07:00'\n   104→\n   105→    >>> local.humanize()\n   106→    'an hour ago'\n   107→\n   108→    >>> local.humanize(locale='ko-kr')\n   109→    '한시간 전'\n   110→\n   111→.. end-inclusion-marker-do-not-remove\n   112→\n   113→Documentation\n   114→-------------\n   115→\n   116→For full documentation, By using it, you agree to cede\n    20→control over minutiae of hand-formatting. In return, _Black_ gives you speed,\n    21→determinism, and freedom from `pycodestyle` nagging about formatting. You will save time\n    22→and mental energy for more important matters.\n    23→\n    24→Blackened code looks the same regardless of the project you're reading. Formatting\n    25→becomes transparent after a while and you can focus on the content instead.\n    26→\n    27→_Black_ makes code review faster by producing the smallest diffs possible.\n    28→\n    29→Try it out now using the [Black Playground](https://black.vercel.app). Watch the\n    30→[PyCon 2019 talk](https://youtu.be/esZLCuWs_2Y) to learn more.\n    31→\n    32→---\n    33→\n    34→**[Read the documentation on ReadTheDocs!](https://black.readthedocs.io/en/stable)**\n    35→\n    36→---\n    37→\n    38→## Installation and usage\n    39→\n    40→### Installation\n    41→\n    42→_Black_ can be installed by running `pip install black`. It requires Python 3.10+ to\n    43→run. If you want to format Jupyter Notebooks, install with\n    44→`pip install \"black[jupyter]\"`.\n    45→\n    46→### Usage\n    47→\n    48→To get started right away with sensible defaults:\n    49→\n    50→```sh\n    51→black {source_file_or_directory}\n    52→```\n    53→\n    54→You can run _Black_ as a package if running it as a script doesn't work:\n    55→\n    56→```sh\n    57→python -m black {source_file_or_directory}\n    58→```\n    59→\n    60→Further information can be found in our docs:\n    61→\n    62→- [Usage and Configuration](https://black.readthedocs.io/en/stable/usage_and_configuration/index.html)\n    63→\n    64→_Black_ is already [successfully used](https://github.com/psf/black#used-by) by many\n    65→projects, small and big. _Black_ has a comprehensive test suite, with efficient parallel\n    66→tests, and our own auto formatting and parallel Continuous Integration runner. Now that\n    67→we have become stable, you should not expect large formatting changes in the future.\n    68→Stylistic changes will mostly be responses to bug reports and support for new Python\n    69→syntax. For more information please refer to\n    70→[The Black Code Style](https://black.readthedocs.io/en/stable/the_black_code_style/index.html).\n    71→\n    72→Also, as a safety measure which slows down processing, _Black_ will check that the\n    73→reformatted code still produces a valid AST that is effectively equivalent to the\n    74→original (see the\n    75→[Pragmatism](https://black.readthedocs.io/en/stable/the_black_code_style/current_style.html#ast-before-and-after-formatting)\n    76→section for details). If you're feeling confident, use `--fast`.\n    77→\n    78→## The _Black_ code style\n    79→\n    80→_Black_ is a PEP 8 compliant opinionated formatter. _Black_ reformats entire files in\n    81→place. Style configuration options are deliberately limited and rarely added. It doesn't\n    82→take previous formatting into account (see\n    83→[Pragmatism](https://black.readthedocs.io/en/stable/the_black_code_style/current_style.html#pragmatism)\n    84→for exceptions).\n    85→\n    86→Our documentation covers the current _Black_ code style, but planned changes to it are\n    87→also documented. They're both worth taking a look at:\n    88→\n    89→- [The _Black_ Code Style: Current style](https://black.readthedocs.io/en/stable/the_black_code_style/current_style.html)\n    90→- [The _Black_ Code Style: Future style](https://black.readthedocs.io/en/stable/the_black_code_style/future_style.html)\n    91→\n    92→Changes to the _Black_ code style are bound by the Stability Policy:\n    93→\n    94→- [The _Black_ Code Style: Stability Policy](https://black.readthedocs.io/en/stable/the_black_code_style/index.html#stability-policy)\n    95→\n    96→Please refer to this document before submitting an issue. What seems like a bug might be\n    97→intended behaviour.\n    98→\n    99→### Pragmatism\n   100→\n   101→Early versions of _Black_ used to be absolutist in some respects. They took after its\n   102→initial author. This was fine at the time as it made the implementation simpler and\n   103→there were not many users anyway. Not many edge cases were reported. As a mature tool,\n   104→_Black_ does make some exceptions to rules it otherwise holds.\n   105→\n   106→- [The _Black_ code style: Pragmatism](https://black.readthedocs.io/en/stable/the_black_code_style/current_style.html#pragmatism)\n   107→\n   108→Please refer to this document before submitting an issue just like with the document\n   109→above. What seems like a bug might be intended behaviour.\n   110→\n   111→## Configuration\n   112→\n   113→_Black_ is able to read project-specific default values for its command line options\n   114→from a `pyproject.toml` file. This is especially useful for specifying custom\n   115→`--include` and `--exclude`/`--force-exclude`/`--extend-exclude` patterns for your\n   116→project.\n   117→\n   118→You can find more details in our documentation:\n   119→\n   120→- [The basics: Configuration via a file](https://black.readthedocs.io/en/stable/usage_and_configuration/the_basics.html#configuration-via-a-file)\n   121→\n   122→And if you're looking for more general configuration documentation:\n   123→\n   124→- [Usage and Configuration](https://black.readthedocs.io/en/stable/usage_and_configuration/index.html)\n   125→\n   126→**Pro-tip**: If you're asking yourself \"Do I need to configure anything?\" the answer is\n   127→\"No\". _Black_ is all about sensible defaults. Applying those defaults will have your\n   128→code in compliance with many other _Black_ formatted projects.\n   129→\n   130→## Used by\n   131→\n   132→The following notable open-source projects trust _Black_ with enforcing a consistent\n   133→code style: pytest, tox, Pyramid, Django, Django Channels, Hypothesis, attrs,\n   134→SQLAlchemy, Poetry, PyPA applications (Warehouse, Bandersnatch, Pipenv, virtualenv),\n   135→pandas, Pillow, Twisted, LocalStack, every Datadog Agent Integration, Home Assistant,\n   136→Zulip, Kedro, OpenOA, FLORIS, ORBIT, WOMBAT, and many more.\n   137→\n   138→The following organizations use _Black_: Dropbox, KeepTruckin, Lyft, Mozilla, Quora,\n   139→Duolingo, QuantumBlack, Tesla, Archer Aviation.\n   140→\n   141→Are we missing anyone?   44→========================\n    45→Comprehensive object introspection.\n    46→\n    47→Input history, persistent across sessions.\n    48→\n    49→Caching of output results during a session with 53→Extensible system of ‘magic’ commands for controlling the environment and performing many tasks related to IPython or the operating system.\n    54→\n    55→A rich configuration system with easy
